title: Altman and Amodei’s “unsafe at any prompt” moment for AI
text:
Altman and Amodei’s “unsafe at any prompt” moment for AI

Detroit spent a decade calling crashes driver error. The AI industry is running the same defense, now we’re all sitting in the same seat. Now is a great time to act.

Ralph Nader published Unsafe at Any Speed in 1965. Only one of its eight chapters covers the Corvair, and he lost that part — NHTSA later found the car no more prone to rollover than its competitors i.e. they were as unsafe as just about any other car on the market.

He won the larger argument anyway.

Car deaths were treated as failures of the person behind the wheel, and Nader put them back on the drawing board. That argument is playing out around AI in almost the same words.

The industry has a failure rate it’s working on engineering away, a user base it quietly blames for hitting it in it’s current state, and no shared way to measure the damage.

This is Sam Altman’s and Dario Amodei’s moment more than anyone’s. They run the companies, they hold the capital, and one has already published the case for slowing down — something Detroit’s executives never volunteered.

Quite honestly, they’re trying to do the right thing, and it has to reach the layer where the harm lands on a person, and that layer is the interface.

The Human In The Loop, Er, Behind the Wheel

Detroit’s position through the 1950s was that cars were fine and drivers were the problem. Its shorthand for the cause of a crash was the nut behind the wheel, and the framing did real work: if the driver is the defect, the product doesn’t need to change.

AI has rebuilt that defense out of new parts.

  • A model invents a citation and the explanation is prompting.
  • Someone acts on a wrong answer and it is AI literacy.

Answering a product failure with better messaging is inherited: Sterling Cooper built your UX process, and a discipline raised on persuasion reaches for the campaign when the product is at fault.

The analog is if the driver is the defect, the product doesn’t need to change.

The behavior being blamed is documented. Automation bias has been in the literature since Kathleen Mosier and Linda Skitka named it in the 1990s: people defer to a machine even when it is wrong and the evidence sits in front of them.

The models make it worse. Stanford’s 2026 AI Index found that when a false statement is presented as something the user believes, model performance collapses — the system agrees with you at the moment you need it not to.

Telling people to prompt better is driver education with a different safety record.

The Label Instead of the Redesign

That defense was never a Detroit invention.

America over-pivots on personal responsibility, and the principle is real — adults make their own choices. I’m a social libertarian, so the instinct is mine too, which is why it’s worth being precise about where it stops working.

The disposition is constitutional. The Second Amendment is its sharpest expression: the individual, not the state, is the unit of safety.

The First Amendment runs the same way from the other side: the remedy for bad information is more information, not a constraint on whoever produced it.

Congress turned that instinct into a statute. Section 230 says an online service is not treated as the publisher of what its users post, and courts read it broadly enough that platform harms became speech questions for two decades.

It is the warning label of the internet, and it is why a disclaimer under a prompt box feels like a complete answer because in America, it is.

Which is why the Meta plaintiffs stopped litigating speech. Section 230 shields a company for what someone else wrote. It does not shield the design of the machine that decided who saw it.

https://medium.com/media/547c0281a140e9afca055675912183c5/href

Thank You for Smoking played it as comedy, seating tobacco, alcohol, and firearms lobbyists in one booth, the tobacco man running on one principle — “if you argue correctly, you’re never wrong.”

The label was not a defeat for the industry. It was the containment.

Cigarettes are the clearest case, though The Jungle got there first in 1906. The Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act of 1965 required a caution line on every pack while barring anyone else from imposing a stronger one for four years.

The label was the containment, and it held: smokers sued for four decades and almost never won, because the defense was that they knew and chose.

The wall broke in 1998, with the Tobacco Master Settlement Agreement. Firearms got the reflex written into statute: the Sandy Hook families only got through on the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act’s marketing exception, winning on how the rifle was advertised rather than built.

Alcohol runs the same structure on two words. Drink responsibly.

That reframing is the newest instance. In March 2026 a New Mexico jury found Meta violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act over child safety, and a day later a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube negligent on the theory that the harm came from design choices.

Jurors saw the documents and agreed.

Nobody Gets a Letter

Fight Club put the arithmetic on screen. The narrator coordinates recalls: cars in the field, times the rate of failure, times the average out-of-court settlement.

https://medium.com/media/52ca5a9e450798720fcf9d6278e3e66c/href
If a new car built by my company leaves Chicago traveling west at 60 miles per hour, and the rear differential locks up, and the car crashes and burns with everyone trapped inside, does my company initiate a recall?
You take the population of vehicles in the field [A] and multiple it by the probable rate of failure [B], then multiply the result by the average cost of an out-of-court settlement [C].
A times B times C equals X. This is what it will cost if we don’t initiate a recall.
If X is greater than the cost of a recall, we recall the cars and no one gets hurt.
If X is less than the cost of a recall, then we don’t recall. If X comes in under the cost of a recall, no one is notified.

Chuck Palahniuk didn’t invent that math because Ford ran it.

The Pinto memo priced a burn death at $200,000 and weighed an $11-per-car fuel-tank fix against projected settlements, and the fix lost.

Mother Jones published it in 1977, NHTSA found a defect the next year, Ford recalled 1.5 million cars, and a Grimshaw jury returned $125 million in punitive damages, later cut to $3.5 million.

What matters is how ordinary it was: arithmetic routine enough to file with a regulator. A formula with a zero in it always resolves the same way.

The AI version of that equation is missing a term.

No settlement for a wrong answer, no line item for an incident, no cost landing on the product team when a fabricated number gets acted on. This brings us back to the disclaimer in six-point type under the prompt box.

It shipped before any regulator asked and design reviews run the same way: the room strengthens the disclaimer rather than the thing it apologizes for because that costs more.

The Second Collision

One caveat before the answer. A wrong answer is not a car crash, and nobody dies of a fabricated citation. The parallel is the mechanism, not the body count. Cars are where we learned that a product with a known failure rate gets seat belts and airbags rather than a campaign about careful driving, and the question is what the seat belt is when the failure is a sentence.

Nader’s durable contribution was a distinction borrowed from crash researchers. The first collision is the car hitting something. The second is the body hitting the inside of the car, and in 1965 that interior was styled rather than engineered — a steering column aimed at the chest, chrome knobs at face height.

Engineers stopped trying to prevent the crash and designed the interior around it.

AI has the same two-stage structure, and we talk almost exclusively about the first stage. The model being wrong is the first collision, a property of the machine, and not a small one: the AI Index measured hallucination rates across 26 leading models ranging from 22% to 94%.

That spread is the point. Rates move with the task and how the question is phrased, so any single number is an argument waiting to happen.

Take the best case: a system wrong one time in five is a car leaving the factory without seat belts or brakes, and nobody ships that because most trips end fine.

Designers don’t own the first collision. They own the second one completely.

The second collision is what the interface does with a wrong answer on its way to a person. Confident prose, no visible uncertainty, no citation or one nobody can click, the output pre-filled into the field the user was going to send.

Explainability is the guardrail that does the most work here, and it gets confused with interpretability. What happens inside the model belongs to the labs. Explainability belongs to you: what the answer drew on, which parts are inference, what a person does when it looks wrong.

No one should pretend the upstream half gets solved quickly. Amodei’s own essay concedes that after years of progress, “we still only understand a tiny fraction of what goes on inside these models.”

That is a reason to build the downstream guardrail now, not a reason to wait. The interior got padded while engineers were still arguing about what happens in a crash.

An answer a user can interrogate is an answer they can catch. A flat assertion is the chrome knob.

Christopher Noessel named it years earlier. Designing Agentive Technology argues that systems acting on a person’s behalf live or die on handoff and takeback — the moments where the machine gives control back and the person can take it. Most AI features ship without either half.

Nobody Crash-Tests the Interface

Before crash testing, a buyer compared horsepower, zero to sixty, and price. Safety had no number, so it lost every argument inside the company.

AI is in that period now. The AI Index found almost every frontier developer reports capability benchmarks while responsible AI reporting stays sparse. The Foundation Model Transparency Index average fell from 58 to 40 and incidents in the AI Incident Database rose to 362 in 2025 from 233, while adoption reached 88%.

Capability has a leaderboard. Harm has a mailing list.

A crash test for an interface is not exotic. Seed prompts where the model is wrong, run real users through the feature, count how many wrong answers reach a consequential action.

Call it the wrong-answer survival rate.

I do this to my own work, including this piece. Everything AI-assisted I publish runs inside a harness: a rule set, a script that fails the output on violations, a score I clear before it ships. A seat belt, worn because I assume the crash.

Nobody at GM Invited the Auditors In

General Motors was not surprised by anything Nader wrote. Test data, memos, and a revised rear suspension in 1964 all predate the book. His act was publication.

The same asymmetry defines AI. Red-teaming happens constantly, but the AI Index notes it is rarely disclosed against a common set of benchmarks.

Teams know where their systems fail; everyone else is guessing.

Designers hold a version nobody else has: the session where a participant accepted an invented figure because it arrived fast and certain. Mike Monteiro put it plainly in A Designer’s Code of Ethics: a designer is responsible for the work they put into the world.

We can all act the same.

In September 2026, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei published We Must Pace the Frontier, arguing capability advancement should be slowed and committing the company to embedded third-party evaluators such as METR, with desks, badges, and the right to publish findings it cannot redact for being unfavorable.

Nobody at GM offered Ralph Nader a desk, a badge, and a laptop. Thankfully, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman’s can and should.

Within hours Jim Clyde Monge read it as the start of an industry-wide slowdown call rather than one company’s position, and Altman said OpenAI would match it: “we will do the same.”

He also swings at the recall formula: dismissing a multi-agent incident because its damage was small is the mistake, an argument against pricing harm by what it already cost.

Give them both the credit.

Saying it is also the cheapest thing either can do: Anthropic closed a $65 billion round near a trillion-dollar valuation and Altman’s OpenAI was valued at $852 billion, so the constraint is what they choose to build next.

Amodei is doing the right thing, and the evaluator commitment is the right shape: unilateral, costly, made before anyone required it. The harder test is whether safety survives as an economic decision rather than an essay. Corporate responsibility is not a position on risk.

It is a line in a budget and a revenue number someone agreed to make smaller.

And read the plan for where design appears. Evaluators, checkpoints, interpretability, alignment training, compute limits — every lever sits upstream of the model. Pacing slows the labs, not the teams assembling interfaces on top of what already shipped.

Your team still ships Thursday.

Standards Slip, Ship Dates Don’t

The legislative half is fast and then slow. The book landed in 1965, the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act passed in 1966, and the fight over passive restraints ground into the 1980s. AI is following: under the Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the AI Act’s high-risk obligations moved to Dec. 2, 2027.

In America the statute is what shows up instead of the responsibility.

Explainability is already law in two places.

  • Under the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 13 requires high-risk systems to be transparent enough that deployers can interpret their output, and Article 86 gives anyone affected the right to a clear explanation.
  • California got there through privacy law: the California Consumer Privacy Act now carries automated decision-making rules — pre-use notice, access to the logic, a human appeal — due Jan. 1, 2027.

Explanation is not arriving because product teams decided users deserve one, it is arriving on a compliance calendar.

Europe runs it in a different order. From Dec. 9, 2026, Directive (EU) 2024/2853 treats software and AI as products under strict, no-fault liability, and a company cannot contract out of it. In the U.S. the same system is a service governed by an agreement the user clicked through.

That reads as European companies being more responsible. I read it as Europe writing the duty down first while America waits for case law — the EU delayed its own deadline by 16 months under the same arguments Detroit used.

What Europe is better at is refusing to let the duty depend on it.

Detroit did not pad the dashboard until a law said to. Tobacco did not label the pack until Congress wrote the sentence. In America the statute shows up instead of the responsibility, later than the harm and usually narrower.

It also worked. In 1966, 50,894 people died on U.S. roads, a rate of 5.5 per 100 million miles traveled. By 2024 NHTSA estimated 39,345 deaths at a rate of 1.20, on vastly more miles.

The Argument You Can Actually Win

What Nader moved was the location of responsibility. Once crashes became design outputs they became measurable, and then they got engineered down for 60 years. AI is sitting at that hinge, missing only the crash test. Regulators will get there 16 months late, and your team will ship 40 releases before they do.

The discipline that padded the dashboard is the one reading this. Pick the second collision up, because nobody is going to hand it to you.

The Action Items

Whose job is this? The discipline that solved it last time is holding it now.

Padded dashboards and collapsible columns came from human-factors research — people who studied what bodies do in a crash rather than what drivers ought to do to avoid one. That field is the direct ancestor of user experience.

The skillset transfers: watching what people do rather than what the spec assumes, specifying the states nobody wants to think about, making a risk concrete enough to survive a launch review.

Dan Maccarone put the professional question the right way round in Craft vs. Complacency: the challenge isn’t staying ahead of the robots, it’s “how do we stay accountable to our users, our teams, and ourselves?”

A discipline that answers that question is doing the job. One that answers the first is doing tool training.

The method exists in the field’s literature. sheryl cababa gives a chapter of Closing the Loop to anticipating unintended consequences, on the grounds that user-centered design looks only at the person holding the product — the blind spot that lets a bad output travel.

  • Engineering owns the happy path.
  • Legal owns the exposure and arrives after the decision.
  • Research and design are the only functions whose method is the gap between intended use and real use — where the second collision happens.

Here’s the checklist.

  • Write the second collision into the spec. State what happens when the output is wrong, not how often it is right.
  • Measure wrong-answer survival. Put that rate on the same dashboard as adoption.
  • Pad the interior. Inline citations, visible uncertainty, cheap undo, a pause before anything auto-sends.
  • Publish the memo internally. Bring the clip of someone accepting a fabricated answer to the launch review, with the frequency attached.
  • Ship the explanation before the calendar demands it. The CCPA rules require a version by January 2027 and Article 86 requires it in the EU. Building early is free compliance and better product.

Altman and Amodei’s “unsafe at any prompt” moment for AI was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Please don’t stretch your app for foldables
text:
Please don’t stretch your app for foldables

What happens when the screen isn’t a fixed constraint?

Foldables have existed in the market since 2019 with the Samsung Galaxy Fold, but it’s really only been an “Android thing.” And if your app primarily serves the U.S. market (where most smartphones are iOS), foldables haven’t been a priority to design for. Even with an Android customer base, only a small percentage of those devices are foldables.

But this foldable conversation is different now with Apple’s iPhone Duo announcement. This one foldable has caused more buzz than the entire Android foldable ecosystem ever has.

If you’ve never considered designing for foldables for your native app experience, it’s understandable (and common). It’s hard to get design/engineering buy-in when so few people will use the app on such a unique form factor.

Now there’s a greater argument. iPhone Duo has a strong sales forecast and is projected to take 25% of the foldable market by end of 2026; only to increase from there.

So if you’re starting from square-one and have no idea how to address foldables, it’s good to have a foundation to both understand the form factor and the expectations between iOS and Android. Let’s get into some best practices to integrate iOS and Android foldables into your design process.

Core principles

Foldables seem complex because they combine multiple screen sizes, aspect ratios, orientations, and postures in a single device. To maintain a good experience with foldables, you need to adapt hierarchy, layout, and controls to the available space and how the device is being used (don’t worry, we’ll get there).

Design for available space vs. the device

Instead of asking “What does this screen look like on a Galaxy Z Fold/iPhone Duo?”, ask “What does this experience need to do when the available window becomes wider, narrower, taller, or split?”

The same designs should be able to accommodate:

  • Standard phones
  • Flip and book-style foldables
  • Tablets or multitasking windows

Preserve hierarchy

When available space changes, the UI doesn’t need to remain visually identical.

What should adapt:

  • Navigation & control placement
  • Content density / amount of content displayed
  • Number of columns
  • Supporting information / image size

What should not adapt:

  • Primary task & key actions
  • Content hierarchy
  • Navigation model & user’s current context

For example:

When the iPhone Duo is closed, content is presented in a drill-down style with List → Tap → Detail. Versus when opened, the same content is presented simultaneously with the list on the left and details on the right of the device.

Don’t stretch the UI

You may think allowing the UI layout to expand across a large device display is an easy solution to fill in the space, but Android specifically asks for the usage of panes and adaptive layouts.

Best practices:

  • Add maximum content widths & larger gutters between elements
  • Use multiple columns & supporting panes
  • Ensure grids are responsive

Avoid:

  • Extremely long text lines (line length should be about 50 characters)
  • Oversized cards, modals, bottom sheets, and imagery
  • Full-width buttons spanning a tablet-sized display
  • Excessive empty space

Design around the hinge

Depending on the device, the hinge (where the device folds) can impact touch interactions, content readability, and available layout space.

Avoid positioning important content across the hinge, like:

  • Buttons or form fields (especially critical navigation controls)
  • Dialogs or menus
  • Important text or imagery

Since the hinge’s crease is quite visible in some foldables, it’s best to look at the hinge as the device’s “natural divider.” Both Android and iOS recommend making layouts “hinge-aware,” and to adapt layouts around it.

Think in “panes”

A useful mental model when designing for foldables is:

  • Traditional phone → 1 primary pane
  • Opened foldable/tablet → 2+ related panes

Common layout patterns using panes include:

  • List → detail: Use for search results, messages/emails, or settings
  • Navigation → content: Use when persistent navigation becomes valuable on a larger display
  • Primary content → supporting content/controls: Useful for media, maps, or forms

Understand foldable states

A foldable can have different experiences depending on how it is positioned (called “poses” on iOS and “postures” on Android).

Closed (folded)

The device behaves more like a traditional phone, and uses the outer display of the foldable.

Prioritize what you typically would for native-mobile experiences, like:

  • Essential information & primary/quick actions
  • Compact navigation
  • One-handed interactions

Example display layout:

  • Email inbox list → Tap → Individual email details

Open (flat)

The device provides more space compared to the closed state, and uses the inner displays (they open like a book or clam-shell).

Use the additional space to:

  • Reduce navigation steps & increase content visibility
  • Provide persistent navigation & show additional controls
  • Reveal supporting information by introducing a second pane

Example display layout (for book-style):

  • Email inbox list (left pane) | Individual email details (right pane)

Half-open (tabletop)

The device is partially folded along the hinge in portrait orientation, which creates an upper and lower region.

  • Upper region: Used for content, video, or information
  • Lower region: Used for controls or additional interactions that correspond to the upper region

Example display layout:

  • Upper region includes a video, and lower region includes the playback controls (how Netflix may appear)
Note: This state may not be needed for all experiences; it’s more of an enhancement if the product could benefit from supporting it (i.e., watching videos or playing games).

Half-open (book)

The device is partially folded along the hinge in landscape orientation, and creates two distinct regions in the left and right screens (like a split view).

This state works well for:

  • Reading or reference content for related pieces of info
  • List → detail views
  • Navigation → content views

Example display layouts are similar to the “open” state, but content is divided by the device hinge. This can be used to run 2 apps simultaneously.

Adapt to changing configurations

A user can be in the middle of a task and decide to change their foldable’s orientation (landscape → portrait) or posture (folded → unfolded). When this happens, the app’s navigation, controls, sheets, and other interactive elements need to adapt while preserving the user’s context and maintaining platform conventions.

The same task should remain available across configurations, but you need to define how the presentation responds to best use the available space.

Navigation

Compact view:

  • Use mobile navigation patterns (bottom nav, nav stacks, and back navigation)
  • Keep frequently used navigation within reach

Expanded view:

  • Use persistent navigation, navigation rails, or side navigation
  • Do not stretch mobile navigation patterns across a large display

When the device changes configuration:

  • Preserve the user’s current location, info hierarchy, and navigation state
  • Don’t unexpectedly reset the navigation stack

Sheets, dialogs & overlays

Compact view:

  • Use bottom sheets and full-screen presentations for focused tasks
  • Keep actions within comfortable reach

Expanded view:

  • Use centered dialogs, partial-width sheet, side panel, or secondary panes
  • Don’t stretch a mobile sheet or dialog to fill the entire display
  • Avoid placing important content or controls across the fold

Transitions

The transition animation from folded → unfolded should feel continuous and not increase cognitive load.

Prioritize:

  • Preserve state and context
  • Animate meaningful repositioning to keep the user’s focus
  • Maintain content hierarchy

Avoid:

  • Full-screen reloads or loss of scroll position
  • Resetting navigation or form fields
  • Abruptly changing the user’s task

Platform specific guidance

iOS

Apple’s new foldable guidelines introduce several concepts you should consider in your design process. Apple’s arrangement APIs help create layouts that dynamically respond to size and aspect ratio.

For these APIs to work best, you need to define layout rules, size classes, reserved regions, and how components reflow when the device state changes.

I. Use “size classes”

Size classes indicate how much horizontal and vertical space is available to an iOS app’s interface. For foldables, design around Compact and Regular size classes vs. creating custom designs for each pose.

  • Compact: Horizontal=Narrow, Vertical=Short
  • Regular: Horizontal=Wide, Vertical=Tall

II. Respect “reserved regions”

iPhone Duo has physical areas, called reserved regions, that can affect usable space. This is similar to safe areas (like the system UI) in Apple’s ecosystem, and includes the hinge and outer/inner display cameras.

Your design needs to account for the device’s reserved regions, hinge, and safe areas to determine what area is available to your app content.

Note: If you’re interested in learning more about designing for iPhone Duo, Apple has released some helpful, short videos (‘Get ready for iPhone Duo’).

Android

Android’s adaptive design guidelines are built around the available app window vs. physical screen size. The window size can change when a device is unfolded, rotated, or used in multi-window mode, so layouts must respond to the space available to the app.

I. Use “window size classes”

Android’s window size classes determine how your layout should adapt as the available app window changes; similar to iOS size classes.

  • Compact: Narrow phone-sized window
  • Medium: Larger phone or unfolded foldable-sized window
  • Expanded: Tablet-sized or large foldable window

II. Design for “edge-to-edge” and window-insets

Android uses edge-to-edge layouts, with edge-to-edge enforced for apps targeting Android 15 (API 35) and later. Use window-insets to account for system UI and other areas, like camera cutouts, that can overlap your content. Window-insets are similar to the “reserved regions” in iOS.

Consider insets for:

  • Status and navigation bars
  • Display cutouts (cameras–placement differs per device manufacturer)
  • System gestures (swiping left or right from the far edge → Android “Back” action)
  • On-screen keyboard
Note: If you don’t have access to an Android device, you can download “Android Studio” and use the ‘Virtual Device Manager” to access Google Pixel devices ranging between form factors.

Foldable design checklist

Here are some questions to review as you create designs for all different types of device configurations. Once designs are implemented, it’s ideal to pressure test your app in each device configuration (folded, unfolded, half-open, split screen, & portrait/landscape orientations).

Layout

  • Are maximum content widths defined vs. stretching?
  • Does content reflow appropriately?
  • Are different aspect ratios and orientations supported?

Fold / hinge

  • Do important content and UI controls avoid the fold?
  • Do dialogs and sheets avoid the fold?
  • Are controls reachable in every configuration?

Navigation

  • Does navigation adapt to available space?
  • Does the user maintain their place when unfolding or folding?
  • Is navigation still understandable when the window is resized?

Content

  • Does content remain understandable when moved?
  • Are text lines constrained for readability?
  • Do images maintain appropriate aspect ratios?

Foldables aren’t just bigger screens. They introduce multiple ways for people to use the same device, and your app needs to adapt to those possibilities without making the experience feel unfamiliar or unexpected.

So please don’t stretch your app to fill the space. Design for the space that’s available.

Please don’t stretch your app for foldables was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Rethinking writing in the world of design and AI
text:
Rethinking writing in the world of design and AI

What 100 articles taught me about thinking, friction, and the Shoggoth on the horizon

I can’t believe it. I have finally written my 100th design article. What was thought to be an impossible task when I first picked up the pen (or the keyboard) back in 2022 proved to be wrong. Today, I can finally claim a huge sense of achievement and relief. Not because I am done with writing — far from it — but because I continue to have much to say about design.

And as I write a new article every fortnightly, I come to understand myself a little better. The past me isn’t the same as the present me and most likely won’t be the same as the future me. How I think, how I feel, and how I act on those thoughts and emotions have changed too. Oscar Wilde says it best:

If you cannot write well, you cannot think well. And if you cannot think well, others will do your thinking for you.”

These days, the fear of not thinking well has not gone away. You might think that after writing 100 articles, I have the mettle of regurgitating new ideas into prose, that I have a magic box tucked away in my mind that could summon the most original thinking. I have none of those. Instead, I feel like one of the scared crews in Homer’s Odyssey, wondering what monster lurks on the island and when my hero’s journey ends.

In 2026, that boss-level monster on the horizon isn’t a mythical Cyclops. It’s something far more amorphous. I like to call it the Shoggoth: a sprawling entity with grotesque tentacles spilling out of its body while donning a placid, smiling mask. If this is new to you, the Shoggoth originates from the imagination of science-fiction writer H.P. Lovecraft. As writer Jürgen Gravestein puts it, they are shapeshifting creatures created as an instruction-following, slave-like workforce, always under their creators’ control. A bit like large language models. And if you squint really hard, you might actually see the logo of Claude.

I admit. As a designer and a writer, I have a love-hate relationship with AI. I love it for the pseudo-intellectual discourse I have with a sycophant agent. With its seductive charm and frictionless vibing, I could easily generate an article in an evening with a few prompts, saving me time to spend it with my family or doom scrolling on social media (with my wife).

And yet I hate it for how I have fallen prey to deceptive seamlessness without the same struggle of writing that my past self used to experience with the first few articles before ChatGPT. What made this ironic is that while technology is meant for good, the struggle is equally virtuous. Isn’t that what learning is about?

Some designers may view the struggle of writing as a waste of time, thus resorting to AI for quick fixes in their portfolio and work. I tend to agree that AI is a gamechanger for pointless emails. What I am more cautious about is whether we should outsource everything to AI. As Wildes framed it, do we want AI to do the thinking for us?

Anyone who reads and writes about design would know about Fabric Teixeira’s writing. As the co-founder of UX Collective, he advocates for designers to write because not only does our portfolio become multi-dimensional beyond pixels, but it also sharpens our craft and brings communities together. His view on AI is just as valid:

“The value of your actual voice, your real stories, your screw-ups, and your wins are even more valuable. The need for genuine human perspectives has never been higher.”

In many ways, this echoes the exact point of Michael Bierut’s legendary 100-Day Project. Bierut taught us that discipline is the ultimate vehicle for creative inspiration and that real growth only happens when we embrace the friction of repetition. My four-year timeline may have stretched his original design sprint of 100 days, but the core lesson remains identical: by refusing to outsource the labour of thinking, I forced myself to evolve.

What 100 articles taught me

My attention is now on how I will write my next 100 articles. In the world of AI, new designers may face a greater challenge of starting. Experienced writers also face similar challenges of sustaining. While there isn’t any silver bullet that will get you to the habit of writing, there can be ways of finding yourself in the process by learning from others.

Here are some lessons as I found my way into writing for myself:

Motivation

Somehow I knew I could share a point of view in my early days during design critique sessions. The problem was not taking the courage to write consistently, partly due to an imposter syndrome that lingered in my professional career. What became a breakthrough was after a spell as the head of design at Singapore Airlines, where I feared losing the intricate feelings I had in the best (and worst) times in an amazing organisation. This led me to write for myself with a goal of remembering. Over time, that same motivation grew into joy as I would revisit my older self through past articles. It was also uplifting to know that my words will become my legacy if my children ever read the rambling of their father. When the motivation is personal, its intrinsic value carries you forward.

Rethinking success beyond the corporate stairs in the world of design

Space

I needed to experiment with what the optimal conditions were to bring out the best writings. For me, most of my writing happens at home in my kid’s room as they fall asleep. As a design manager in my day job, time is precious, leaving me with a 2–3 hour window every night to type with my smartphone. It also turns out to be the right moment for my flow state to kick in. When it came to tooling, I had tried various tools but eventually stuck with Google Keep for drafts, Canva for visuals and Mybib for reference compilations. I chose these tools for their simplicity to focus on my content. I would then submit my entries to UX Collective or Bootcamp before the editors publish within the next 1–2 days. This became a good rhythm of writing 2 articles every month and being pleasantly surprised whenever the articles get featured in the subsequent weekly newsletter. It gave me space and time to think and reflect on the next set of content.

It's time for dimensional thinking in design

Voice

Turning voice into words can be tricky because every writer has a unique voice. I neither major in literature nor did well academically, which led me to adopt a ‘hacker’ or ‘heck-care’ mindset in putting words together. So I tend to be surprised when I occasionally see virality in some of my articles. One of my earliest hits was my rendition of the atomic design using Eame’s Power of Ten in 2022. LinkedIn and Medium lit with reactions and comments, and I glowed with pride. It didn’t last long, as my next articles went back to normality soon enough. My takeaway? Keep experimenting and finding your authentic voice. For the writer who continues to write will gradually find what resonates with them and their readers. I no longer fish for the next viral topic. Instead, I share what’s top of mind to me as a designer, offering an alternate analogous or contrarian view. That golden thread permeates topics around Figma, rethinking design or fighting a case against AI with human values.

It's time for design to think less and feel more

Authenticity

I wasn’t writing to make a living but to freely express myself. My articles were low-stake playgrounds where I would go on a wild ride. This was my channel to defy difficult stakeholders who preferred to stick to conventions. It was even my creative outlet where I didn’t need to align with my design leaders or direct reports. Sometimes, there can be nasty comments. A small number of them are valid, but more often, they are there because someone has something to say. What mattered was staying true to the perspective I was building. Over time, I realised that critique is just proof that something resonated enough to provoke a reaction. Writing authentically meant being okay with not pleasing everyone, so long as I didn’t dilute my own perspective.

Liquid Glass isn't a design failure; it is Apple's most tactile digital future yet

Forgiveness

There are definitely bad days where the mental block persists. Perhaps due to overwhelming work or an unsolvable problem, writing anything about design just didn’t happen. I dreaded those days because my sense of control slipped away. Other times were the loss of concentration or the nearly captured idea, only to reach a dead end. Trust me: there were drafts that never saw light because I lost the plot. Doing the maths will clearly show that there were dry seasons of no articles for weeks. I will admit that writing with AI came in. Not those that fix grammatical errors, but those that generate essays from a few prompts. So while I may think I could get away with slop, the funny thing about good publications is that they have seen enough AI slop entries to detect an article from the distance. My sins are exposed. My circumstances are unknown. It took forgiveness of my lack of actions and from my editors, who knew my work over the years, to move forward. Today, I still use AI for my work, but I no longer outsource my thinking to a soulless entity. I would put writing aside if nothing is coming out, and that’s okay.

How loss is experienced by designers and 10 tips to find yourself again

Joy

Let’s play a game. What if we could predict the next Pantone colour of the year? What will be the next Star Wars articles about design on May the Fourth (be with you)? Or how about the next article about circles on March 14 (3.14)? Joy is the most important lesson of being alive. Studying design in France taught me the seriousness of playful poetry. My design boss amplified the same point by acknowledging that a designer’s mood reflects the quality of the work. How true it is when you are having fun with concepts. Or a serendipitous conversation that became an entire essay. Creative writing doesn’t necessarily follow a formula. Instead, the idea ends up as writing, appreciated by people.

Why we need to have a change of HEART with UX metrics

Tribe

I had been very lucky these past 4 years. I still wonder how my first few articles were picked up by my editors. However, I stopped questioning and continued to trust the process. More importantly, writing has helped me connect with some of the most amazing designers. It has truly brought me to places unimaginable, both physically and cognitively. One such example was writing about Design 4.0, as the fourth industrial revolution in design connected me to Ilona Gurjanova, former president of the Estonian Association of Designers. Little did I know I was off to Estonia as a keynote speaker for the Tallinn Design Festival. Or how my work on modular journey maps ended up in Miroverse with more than 2000 views. Or the topic of design feeling transporting itself to platforms like DOC and the state of UX. Along with the countless mentions, reposts, comments and featured newsletters, I feel like I have found my design tribe beyond the island that I am living on. And that tribe is carrying me on to my next adventure.

What an accessibility conference taught me about designing for all

Homer wrote in Odyssey that each man delights in the work that suits him best. I’m glad to take the plunge of writing on topics that I am still in love with, even though the blank page is no less intimidating than it was in 2022. The Shoggoth of AI will continue to evolve, tempt, and disrupt how we create and think. But if these past four years have taught me anything, it’s that the virtue of writing isn’t in the output… It’s in the friction of the process.

We don’t write merely to produce words; we write to figure out who we are and what we believe in. So here’s to the next 100 articles, the next 100 struggles, and every quiet late-night insight along the way. I look forward to etching my thoughts in the present as memories for the future.

References

I Went to Banff To Say Yes To Everything
text:
I Went to Banff To Say Yes To Everything
If you’re looking for a reason to switch on your out-of-office reply, we’ve got you covered. Wellbeing-driven, wanderlust-focused, our travel series takes you to places worth the trip, not only to escape the grind, but to spark some joy, reset, recover, and return ready for whatever’s next. Let us show you the world.

I arrived in Canada with a smile. I had packed exactly the right amount of underwear, my clothes were coordinated, and I had definitely remembered toothpaste. As a chaotic Type B traveler, this was growth, and the right start to what was supposed to be a relaxing trip in the mountains. 

I’d been invited by Moxy Banff and Marriott Bonvoy Moments for three days of exploring the Canadian Rockies, from Lake Louise and Moraine Lake to the Bow River. 

But I had also arrived carrying something I hadn’t packed: the lingering feeling that I should always be doing more. 

My life revolves around work, deadlines, and an endless stream of notifications, and I had gotten very good at being productive and increasingly bad at being present. Even on vacation, part of me was usually thinking about what needed to happen next. 

Somewhere along the hour-long drive to Moxy Banff, surrounded by mountains and increasingly spotty cell service, I decided whatever was waiting for me back home could wait. 

It was time to fully go out of office. 

My Wishes for This Trip 

As I settled into my flight and gazed out the window in the kind of dreamlike state only a Pisces could understand, I took a deep breath and set two intentions for the trip. 

Number one: Become more present. I wanted to enjoy the little moments. The bees landing on flowers, the textures, and the moments I would one day wish I could get back. To push me to do so, I brought my camera. Photography used to be one of the main ways I made sense of the world before it became something I was always too busy to do. On this trip, my camera would become my North Star. 

Number two: Do some scary sh*t. Before the trip even started, I knew kayaking was on the itinerary. Through Marriott Bonvoy Moments, the entire experience had already been planned for us, from where we’d go to the people we’d get to experience it with. It was the kind of access that made trying something completely outside of my comfort zone feel a little more possible. 

And as a proud mammal who can’t even swim, voluntarily paddling down the Bow River felt slightly unhinged. Better yet, unnatural. 

To raise the stakes, Marriott invited two-time Olympian Evy Leibfarth to join us. Yes, the Evy Leibfarth, the first American woman to medal in Olympic canoe slalom after taking bronze in the women’s C1 event at the 2024 Paris Games. 

So, yes, the stakes felt pretty high. Still, I wanted to do it. The goal wasn’t to suddenly become fearless; it was to stop allowing fear to keep me from truly living. I would leave Banff with at least one new skill and that was enough. 

What I Packed 

For once in my life, I actually packed according to the itinerary. With only three days in Banff, I kept things simple and leaned heavily on Oner Active’s Lori Harvey Day-to-Night Capsule: the SoftMotion Racerback Dress for hiking, plus the Soft Motion Straight Leg Pants and matching High Waisted Leggings for everything in between.  

I also packed for the important business of smelling good. During the day, I wore Blank Body Sculpt Body Oil in Sweet Plantain, a warm, plantain scent that felt surprisingly fitting for the mountains. I also paired it with Vaseline’s Sunlit Glow Body Shimmer Gel Oil for extra hydration. At night, I switched to my Phlur Island Swim body mist. 

However, if I could go back and repack, I’d grab a heavier coat. Sure, the daytime was warm, but at night, my little airport hoodie was not going to cut it. And Banff is the kind of place you want to walk around and take in, so don’t let being a little chilly cut your night short. 

Day 1 

Banff, for the record, is not a real place. 

It’s the kind of town you’d imagine being dropped off somewhere along the Polar Express route. The entire town is framed by mountains, so no matter which direction you look, there’s this absurdly beautiful backdrop behind everything. 

Our home for the weekend, Moxy Banff, somehow fit right into all of it. The hotel had this retro, mid-century mountain-lodge feel that made it playful without letting you forget you were surrounded by the Canadian Rockies. After checking in, we dropped our things and walked into town, which took around 20 minutes. As a former New Yorker, this qualified as basically next door. 

That evening, I found myself at Pizzeria Sophia, eating the best lemon pasta of my life. I struck up a conversation with my server, who was from Australia. He was working at the restaurant while training to become a snowboard instructor. 

Over the next three days, I would meet person after person who had come to Banff for the same reason: there was something here they loved enough to rearrange their lives around. They were people who had moved their entire lives across the world to chase something I would personally categorize as some “scary shit”! Without even realizing it, my wish to do some scary shit was already manifesting, with every person I met showing me what was possible when you stopped letting fear make your decisions. 

Day 2 

Some places are so beautiful your brain has a hard time computing that what you’re looking at is real. Lake Louise was one of them. The water was this almost ridiculous shade of blue, surrounded by mountains so massive that the whole thing looked less like a real place and more like one of those default MacBook screensavers. 

At Moraine Lake, I climbed to a viewpoint overlooking mountains that had existed long before me and would continue existing long after me. Everything felt enormous, and all the little things that normally consumed my attention suddenly felt small. 

I instinctively reached for my phone to take a photo and realized I didn’t have service. 

There were no emails to answer, feeds to refresh, or notifications competing for my attention. Whatever was happening beyond those mountains would have to wait. For the first time in a while, I felt my shoulders loosen and my breath steady. All I had in front of me was the landscape and my camera. 

I photographed the water, the mountains, and the people who appeared impossibly tiny against them. I started noticing composition and light again. I began looking at the world the way I used to, when taking photographs was something I did simply because it made me happy. 

Then I looked down at one of my first images and low-key? 

I still had it. 

Day 3 

If day two was about slowing down, day three was about learning how to say yes, even after I had already said no. 

We set out that morning to kayak the Bow River alongside Evy Leibfarth. I was excited, despite having done absolutely zero research into what kayaking actually entailed. I climbed into a tandem kayak with another girl and almost immediately realized that I had no idea what I was doing. We could not get in sync. Within minutes, we were both frustrated, barely moving, and I was ready to call it, so I got out. 

I had already decided I was good. I could walk, take some pictures, and enjoy the scenery from the very safe comfort of land. But everyone around me kept encouraging me, and eventually they convinced me to try again, this time in my own kayak. 

Once I stopped worrying about throwing someone else off, I found my rhythm. I paddled down the river, surrounded by mountains, passing a beaver dam along the way. I realized the thing I had been terrified to do was actually…peaceful. 

Even our kayaking instructor had moved from England to Banff because he wanted to snowboard. Another person who had crossed an ocean because there was something here he loved enough to follow. 

After kayaking, we met back up with Evy for a multi-course lunch at The Maple Leaf Steak & Seafood. It was the perfect ending for what was supposed to be a terrifying day. Later that afternoon, I wandered through Banff by myself, stopped in museums, took pictures, and followed whatever looked interesting. There was no schedule to check and nowhere I needed to rush off to next. That afternoon, I got to simply exist. 

What to Know Before You Go 

I went in August, which was the right call. The weather was warm enough to spend my days outside, the mountains were still snow-dusted in the distance, and I could hike without having to become a winter-sports person overnight.

You can’t drive a personal car to Moraine Lake. Parks Canada closed Moraine Lake Road to personal vehicles in 2023, so you’ll need to arrange transportation ahead of time. There are several approved shuttle and public transit options available, but reservations can fill up quickly.

Yes, you need a park pass. Banff is inside Banff National Park, which means visitors need a valid Parks Canada park pass. You can purchase one ahead of time or when you arrive, but I’d handle it before the trip so there’s one less thing to think about once you’re there.

Moxy Banff is walkable to downtown. One of my favorite parts of staying at Moxy was being able to walk into town instead of constantly worrying about a car. Downtown Banff is roughly a 20-minute walk from the hotel, so pack comfortable shoes.

Check Marriott Bonvoy Moments before your trip. The kayaking experience I did was available through Marriott Bonvoy Moments, where Marriott Bonvoy members can use points to bid on or redeem experiences that go beyond a traditional hotel stay—from food and music to sports and outdoor adventures.

Bring good walking shoes, some layers, and an itinerary… or don’t. You’ll find something to do either way.

What I Wish I’d Known 

Sometimes, when you’re in this mindset of wanting to heal, it’s easy to start experiencing your life in the third person. I found myself mentally checking in: Am I doing enough? Am I fulfilling the wishes I set for myself? Is this changing me yet? At some point, even healing can become another thing to accomplish. I wish I’d known that being present is actually much simpler than that. Sometimes, it’s just losing service on a hike and not panicking about it. Letting the email wait. Letting yourself look around without needing to document, respond to, or make meaning out of every second. 

Eventually, I would have to go home, open my laptop, and return to real life. The emails, deadlines, and responsibilities weren’t going anywhere. 

Banff was enough. 

About the Writer 

Jessika Hardy is a freelance writer and social strategist at Refinery29 Unbothered, covering travel, culture, and all things internet. When she’s not online, she’s probably baking banana bread or flipping through records. 

Editor’s note: This trip was hosted by Moxy Banff and Marriott Bonvoy Moments. All opinions and experiences are the writer’s own.

title: I Went to Sensei Lānaʻi to Find My Baseline
text:
I Went to Sensei Lānaʻi to Find My Baseline
If you’re looking for a reason to switch on your out-of-office reply, we’ve got you covered. Wellbeing-driven, wanderlust-focused, our travel series takes you to places worth the trip, not only to escape the grind, but to spark some joy, reset, recover, and return ready for whatever’s next. Let us show you the world. 

I’ve been to Hawaiʻi many times and visited other islands, but Lānaʻi is the one people talk about with deep lore. I’d always wanted to see it for myself, and I’d been obsessing about Sensei Lānaʻi, A Four Seasons Resort. It’s a wellness retreat in the upcountry of the island, and the seclusion and specificity were exactly what I wanted. So I reached out about planning a trip, and worked with their wellbeing team to build an itinerary that met me exactly where I was: exhausted, but full and inspired. It also made room for my fiancée, who was in a similar place in their work life.

I was six months into a new job as SVP of Brand & Content at R29Unbothered, and those months had been a satisfying whirlwind, full of new skills and the strange relief of finally being inside an industry I’ve loved from the outside for years. They had also been six months without a single day off, and it was showing up in small, unglamorous ways. I’d been carrying the same book from room to room for weeks, reading the same page four nights in a row and retaining none of it. I’m also dealing with some ongoing health stuff, chronic pain that has quietly reorganized my life. I needed to find my baseline, or at least remember I had one — and I had a feeling Sensei could help.

My wish for this trip was specific:  I wanted to surrender to nature, stay off my phone, finish the book, and come home knowing more about my body than I knew when I left. I was excited to find out. So my fiancée and I made our way to Lānaʻi.

What I Packed

• A few vintage silk and linen pieces that I could transition in and out of.
• EltaMD UV Daily Hydration+ SPF 50. I don’t leave the house without it, let alone the state.
• Augustinus Bader The Ultimate Soothing Cream. The single thing that has done the most for my literally soothing my dermatitis.
• Marie Veronique Balancing HypoTonic and Barrier Restore Serum. These two products have changed my skin and hold up in any climate.
• My Clyde Swim Bucket hat In Black. Basic enough to live in all day, which is what the property asks of you.
• The Bond-Eye Sofie Triangle and Serenity Brief, both in black
• My HealthyLine TAJ-Mat, the twenty-by-twenty travel size. It’s the heaviest thing in my bag but I have to have it when I travel, just in case I have a pain flare up
• A Terrible Strength: The Hidden Crisis of the Black Womb and Your Survival Guide to Healing by Dr. Kemi Doll. I hadn’t been able to put it down, so I needed to take it with me.

The Days

Day 1
We landed and were fed before anyone asked anything of us. There’s a Nobu on the property, and dinner that first night was the prime tenderloin tobanyaki, with caramelized onions, shiitake and asparagus, all of it deglazed in sake and yuzu soy and still moving in its hot ceramic dish when it reached the table. Nobody handed me an intake form. Nobody asked me about my goals. We ate, and then we walked back through the gardens into the quietest dark I’d been in for a long time. There were critters everywhere, frogs and lizards moving through the leaves, and the whole property had this nighttime ambient noise running underneath it. It helped us both drop in.

Day 2

The next morning I walked out of my room and did what became my daily practice for the rest of the trip, which was to slow all the way down and take in the flora and fauna on the property.

Tropical flowers in bloom everywhere. The colors you move through on that walk do their own kind of healing work before you ever get to the spa or sit down for a wellbeing session.

Then I had what became my breakfast ritual meal the whole trip, this delicious Japanese breakfast with perfectly brined salmon. 

Then I sat down for a private wellbeing session that paired breathwork with biometrics, which meant they clipped a little node to my earlobe and tracked my heart rate variability while I breathed, so I could watch my own nervous system move in real time. I’ve been meditating since I was seventeen. I had never had proof. The practitioner watched the numbers come in and told me that I drop into a parasympathetic state easily, faster, she said, than most people she works with. That was comforting to hear as a longtime meditator. I had never seen the quantitative impact my practice has on my physiology, and I loved finding out. We spent the rest of the day at the pool, doing nothing, on purpose.

Day 3

The next day we rode horses through the wilderness of Lānaʻi. The stables were beautiful, saddles and tack oiled and knolled like a still life, everything set exactly in its place. My horse was named Spirit and he was exceptionally gentle with me. I loved taking in the energy of the island with equine support, and hearing its history from the ranch hand leading the ride. 

Then we had Lomi Lomi massages, side by side. Lomi Lomi is an indigenous Hawaiian massage practice, rhythmic and deeply connective. The closest analog I’ve found is Thai massage. Both are built on momentum rather than stillness. There is rocking, there is stretching, there is very little lying flat and receiving. You move with the practitioner. This is also the practice that made me a person who gets massages at all: in college in South Africa, the bodyworker I saw was a Pacific Islander who specialized in it. Being returned to it two decades later, in the place it came from, allowed me to be reflective about my own journey, and left me in reverence of Hawaiian culture and their unique somatic intelligence.

Day 4
On day four I went clay shooting, which I had never done in my life and turned out to be pretty good at, which was a surprise. Here’s what I didn’t know: shooting is a full body, hyper focused experience. While you’re tracking a target there is simply no room in your head for anything else, and it’s an immediate off switch.
Later that afternoon I tested my VO2 max. If you haven’t come across it, VO2 max is the measure of how much oxygen your body can actually take in and put to use when you’re working hard. It’s the cleanest proxy we have for cardiovascular fitness, and it happens to be one of the better predictors we have of how long and how well you get to live. The test itself was simple. I walked on a treadmill for about eight minutes breathing into an oxygen device, starting off very slow. Because of my chronic pain, they put me on an incline instead of having me run. The chronic pain has cost me cardiovascular fitness, and seeing that arrive on a screen was less painful than I had braced for. The trainer was matter-of-fact about it, which was exactly what I needed. Honestly, I think this was one of the key pieces that helped inform my baseline. Even though I look strong and feel strong, my cardiovascular capacity is really affected right now. Learning my VO2 max helped me understand that there is still so much room for me to get back to a better baseline.

Day 5
I saved Watsu for the last day, because it’s one of my favorite somatic practices. At Sensei Lānaʻi they call it aquatic bodywork. It’s shiatsu performed in water, with weights on your legs so that you float rather than hover, and I am deeply in love with it. It always feels like a return to the most primordial support there is. We did ours in one of the spa hale, the thousand-square-foot structures tucked into the gardens with their own pools. It turned out to be the right way to say goodbye to the property, release the trip, and get myself ready to go home. A beautiful ritual to close on.

What to Know

Before you go

• The remoteness is the whole proposition. You get there on a thirty-minute semi-private flight from Honolulu on Lānaʻi Air, which is included in the stay, and once you’re on Lānaʻi, you’re on Lānaʻi. If you want to be out and about, this isn’t your trip. 
• The property is eighteen and over, which is a good part of why it stays as quiet as it does. 
• Sensei sits up at Kōʻele in the upcountry, while beach access is down at Hulopoʻe Bay at the sister Four Seasons, about thirty minutes away on a shuttle that runs hourly. The two properties feel like different climates, so pack for both.

Wish I’d known

The wellbeing programming is more rigorous than the setting lets on. The grounds are lush enough that you could mistake this for an escapist trip, and then your VO2 max arrives on a screen. If you go the fitness optimization route, be prepared to blend a serene, nutritive environment with hard information about your body: your cardiovascular capacity, your biometrics, how you actually meditate. For some people that’s too much of a juxtaposition. For me it was exactly what I needed. And if you want something even more restorative and less data driven, they have a rest and sleep focused program.
Oh, and my book. I finished the last few pages on the flight home.

About the Writer
Erica Chidi is SVP of Brand & Content at R29Unbothered

If You’re A Pants-And-A-Top Girl, This One Fall Piece Changes The Whole Look

Right now, the one fall trend that fashionistas are keeping on hand for the cooler fall temperatures is the all mighty suede jacket. It’s rare to come across a jacket that feels luxuriously cool and everyday-wear appropriate. Which is why, when you do, you hold on to that versatile wardrobe hero like a prized trophy.

The sumptuous texture was all over the streets during New York Fashion Week, and it’s easy to see why. Suede has a richness that adds instant depth to practically any outfit without making it feel overly styled.

Imagine throwing one over your go-to jeans-and-a-T-shirt combo or bring a modern edge to your workwear trousers. The finishing touch instantly elevates an otherwise casual look without giving off any I’m-trying-too-hard vibes. On the other side of the outfit spectrum, picture pairing one with a lace-trimmed slip dress. It works just as seamlessly, adding a cool finishing touch without distracting from the rest of the look. That’s the beauty of a great suede jacket: It doesn’t shout for attention, no matter how you style it.

There’s a leather collar-trimmed design by Aligne at the top of my wishlist. The zip-up jacket has that made-to-never-go-out-of-style wow factor that helps justify the price over time. Siempre makes one with the silhouette of a blazer and a belted finish. It’ll look incredibly chic with Bermuda shorts and your go-to boots or flared denim and flats. Want something that can carry you from fall into winter? Avec Les Filles has a longline option with a collar that can be flipped up for a true street-style-star finish.

title: These Rainy-Day Chic Outfits Were The Hero Of New York Fashion Week
text:
These Rainy-Day Chic Outfits Were The Hero Of New York Fashion Week

There’s nothing worst then the torment of a rainy day ruining your plans. One thing I’ve learned from this season of New York Fashion Week is to never let a few drops of water stop you from serving up a photo-worthy look. Fellow show goers seem to be on the same page, too. A few simple styling tricks combined with functional accessories can make dressing to impress a cinch, even during a flood watch.

I like to coordinate my umbrella with my outfit. It, after all, becomes part of the look if you’re carrying it around. If you’re doing a bit of walking, which is kind of a non-negotiable in NYC, the right footwear matters. Ahead, you’ll see a combination of cute, timeless rain boots mixed with glamorous yet surprisingly practical shoes that can handle a wet sidewalk without sacrificing the entire outfit.

But the biggest takeaway from NYFW street style? Dressing for bad weather doesn’t mean every single thing you wear needs to be waterproof. Instead, it’s about choosing where to be practical. A rain boot can make a frilly lace dress work in a downpour. A hood can eliminate the need for an umbrella altogether. And sometimes a closed-toe shoe, cropped hem pants, and a really good parasol are enough to get the job done.

Ahead, I’m breaking down five rainy-day outfits worth stealing from the streets of New York Fashion Week — including my own.

DashDividers_1_500x100

This might be my favorite rainy-day styling equation because the contrast is so good. Instead of letting practical green rain boots dictate the rest of the outfit, they’re paired with a delicate white lace dress and cropped trench cape.

It works because nothing is pretending to be something it isn’t. The boots are unapologetically functional. The dress is unapologetically pretty. And the trench bridges the two, giving the look enough structure that the combination feels intentional rather than like someone changed shoes at the last minute.

It’s also the easiest formula here to recreate: Take the outfit you actually wanted to wear, then swap your precious footwear for a great rain boot.

The styling trick: Don’t build your entire outfit around your rain boots. Sometimes the coolest way to wear them is with something completely unexpected.

DashDividers_1_500x100

If there was ever an argument for making the hood part of the outfit, this is it.

Instead of treating rain protection as something to throw on at the last minute, this look builds it directly into the styling. The black hood creates a dramatic frame around the face while allowing those vivid green trousers to remain the focal point. Even better, their cropped, slightly flared silhouette avoids the cardinal rainy-day sin of fabric sweeping across a wet sidewalk.

And while metallic heeled sandals certainly aren’t the first shoes I’d recommend for trekking across Manhattan in a storm, I appreciate a Queen who commits. Fashion Week does occasionally require accepting that practicality has its limits.

The styling trick: A hood or headscarf can function as both rain protection and an accessory, especially when the rest of the outfit is doing something fun.

DashDividers_1_500x100

This is exactly the kind of high-low styling I want to see during Fashion Week. A sporty, oversized track jacket is inherently practical for unpredictable weather (even if it is Saint Laurent), but pairing it with black capri leggings makes the whole thing feel intentional rather than purely functional.

The woven black shoulder bag adds another texture element without competing with the jacket, while the cropped leggings solve the wet-hem problem entirely. It’s also proof that you don’t necessarily need a classic trench to dress for drizzle. A lightweight technical layer can be just as useful (and, in my humble opinion, considerably more interesting).

The styling trick: Let your outerwear handle the weather, then use an unexpected texture underneath to make the outfit feel styled.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Rainy weather has a way of convincing you that the only reasonable outfit involves pants. This look makes a strong argument for ignoring that instinct.

A distressed brown leather bomber gives a colorful button-down and red plaid mini skirt just enough protection without hiding the entire look beneath a traditional raincoat. The chunky clogs are also a smart move: the substantial sole creates some distance between your feet and the sidewalk while playing into the slightly undone, downtown feel of the look.

What really works is the balance. The skirt and bright layers feel playful, while the leather jacket and grounded footwear keep everything from veering into school-uniform territory.

The styling trick: If you’re wearing a mini in the rain, counterbalance the exposed leg with a substantial jacket and sturdy shoe.

I unintentionally put one of my favorite rainy-day rules to the test during NYFW: when puddles are inevitable, keep your hem off the ground. I paired black pleated culottes with a fluid funnel-neck blouse and brown heeled loafers, which gave me all the polish of a trouser-and-heel combination without having to worry about several inches of soaked fabric dragging behind me.

Accessories did most of the heavy lifting here. A slim black belt gave the loose silhouettes some definition, while a long tassel necklace, pearl earrings, and a silk scarf kept all those office-inspired separates from feeling too corporate. And yes, I carried a black umbrella. With an outfit this neutral, anything brighter would have felt like an uninvited plus-one.

The styling trick: When rain is in the forecast, trade floor-skimming trousers for a cropped wide-leg silhouette and stick with a substantial closed-toe shoe.

title: e.l.f.’s New Lip & Cheek Stain Is Sheer, Long-Lasting, & Only $6
text:
e.l.f.’s New Lip & Cheek Stain Is Sheer, Long-Lasting, & Only $6

Our team tests thousands of beauty products, at every price point, 365 days a year, 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Many are fine, some are good — and then there are the ones that are great. My latest impressive beauty discovery comes in the form of e.l.f. Cosmetics’ new Sheer For It Blush Tints, and you’re about to see why.

Available in nine shades and priced at just $6 each — meaning you could theoretically buy the entire lineup for less than the price of a single luxury blush — Sheer For It is a lightweight, buildable cheek tint designed to deliver anything from a barely-there wash of color to a more saturated flush. The range spans soft pinks, berry tones, warm browns, and vibrant reds, with a sheer finish that can be layered to your desired level of intensity. It’s the kind of low-commitment, high-payoff blush that makes a strong case for keeping one in every makeup bag. (Sounds too good to be true, but then again, it’s what we’ve come to expect from the editor-beloved brand.) 

Ahead, three Refinery29 editors put e.l.f.’s Sheer For It Blush Tints to the test to see whether this $6 cheek tint is actually worth the hype. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Shade(s) tested: So Petal, Cherry Cola

“I’ve tried countless lip and cheek tints in my day, so when I tell you I audibly gasped when I swiped on e.l.f.’s Sheer For It, that’s saying something. This feels like a true, watery stain, but packs an impressive amount of pigment. One layer dotted onto cheeks and swiped on lips lends a kiss of color, but after I let that dry, I was able to layer this stuff on really well; two coats left a visible pop of color, and three rendered it as bold as a powder formula. But because it’s so lightweight, three layers still felt like I was wearing nothing. I will say, these set pretty quickly, so my preferred way to apply them was to dot and blend right away since you do not have a lot of play time. I don’t typically love pink shades on me, but So Petal (a cool, mid-tone pink) was surprisingly flattering on my olive skin. Then there was Cherry Cola, a burnt reddish hue that is more of what I typically gravitate towards. As the name suggests, the color payoff mimics what your lips look like after eating a bowl of cherries – flushed but not in a makeup-y way. Both shades lasted all day (even through sweaty workouts and heat waves) and didn’t transfer or disappear after eating or drinking. Consider me seriously impressed.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Senior Writer

DashDividers_1_500x100

Shade(s) tested: Left On Red

“Confession: liquid tints scare me a little. I like to take my time when applying makeup. And some formulas dry far too quickly for me to blend them out evenly, leaving me with pinches of color rather than the plump, juicy, and defined cheeks I’m after. This, however, boasts just the right consistency, meaning it doesn’t lock onto skin as quickly as the others, so I can take my fluffy brush — or a finger, if I’m so inclined — and tap it into the rest of my makeup without panicking. Left On Red lends my light olive skin the perfect natural flush, like I’ve been outside in the cold and my cheeks have become wind-dappled. Rather than swipe, I apply a few dots over my cheeks and use a dense fluffy brush (with a little primer on the bristles first) to make the final result more uniform. I also dust a touch of translucent powder over the top to diffuse. And the staying power! It’s second to none. Other cheek tints either make a hole in my foundation base or disappear within a few hours, but this one clung on until I removed my makeup at the end of the day. I use it on my lips, too.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Beauty Director

DashDividers_1_500x100

Shade(s) tested: Mauve Actually

“At first glance, this liquid blush looked genuinely intimidating. Between its ultra-fluid, watery consistency and deep Onyx hue, I was terrified it was going to splash everywhere and ruin my white top the second I pulled out the applicator. Thankfully, the wand holds onto the formula well, no messy drips in sight.

Because of how rich the pigment looked in the bottle, I started cautiously with two tiny dabs on each cheek. Once blended, however, it seemed to completely disappear into my deep skin tone. Realizing just how sheer and buildable the formula is, I decided to be much more generous. Layer after layer (I ended up doing about four rounds), my skin seemed to absorb it almost like a hydrating moisturizer. As I continued building the color, a soft, subtle rosiness began to show through. Despite how deep the shade appears in the bottle, the formula applies much sheerer than I expected, which gave me plenty of control over the intensity. I preferred building it up for a more noticeable flush, but the lightweight texture made layering easy without feeling heavy on my skin.

Don’t let the dark initial shade intimidate you: for deeper complexions, a heavy hand and multiple layers are key to getting the color payoff to pop. To finish the look, I tapped a bit onto my lips over a brown lip liner, and it created the most flattering, natural rosy flush. If you’re looking for a versatile, multi-use flush of color that’s easy to layer into your routine, grab it—you won’t regret it.”—Alexis Bennett Parker, Shopping Director

title: How Rizos Curls’ Julissa Prado Gets It All Done as a Multi-Hyphenate Latina
text:
How Rizos Curls’ Julissa Prado Gets It All Done as a Multi-Hyphenate Latina

Sponsor Disclaimer: This article and accompanying podcast episode were sponsored by TextNow.

There’s no shortage of rules for how a Latina is supposed to live. Be ambitious, pero no te pases. Make your family proud, but don’t take up too much space. Work hard, but don’t make anyone uncomfortable by wanting more. And if you dare to question any of it? Well, you might just be called “una sinvergüenza.” Sound familiar?

For too long, that word has been used as a shaming tactic to silence us and put us in our so-called place. But what if we reclaim it? To me, being a sinvergüenza is being a woman without shame — living fully, taking up space, speaking our truth, and reclaiming the parts of ourselves we’ve been told to hide. And aren’t we deserving of that? I think so.

That’s why Somos launched Sin Vergüenza, a biweekly podcast for young Latinas who are figuring out how to live their best, most authentic lives, even when the world around us feels anything but easy. Each episode tackles the questions and challenges that come with being a multidimensional Latina today, from mental health, colorism, and dating to career negotiations, buying your first home, and everything in between. We’re bringing in Latina experts who get it to offer the insight, honesty, and guidance we don’t always have access to.

And we’re kicking things off with a conversation we know many of you will resonate with: How the hell are we supposed to get everything done?

According to a 2026 study from the Latino Donor Collaborative and Kantar, 61% of Latinas have multiple streams of income. Whether it’s because of economic uncertainty or a changing work culture, more of us are juggling multiple jobs, side projects, and personal brands. And not all of us are pulling it off. At least, not without burning ourselves out. For some, it’s the pressure to end generational poverty for ourselves and our loved ones. For others, it’s about making room for all the professional and creative parts of ourselves that we refuse to fit into a single box.

Whatever the reason, the work — and the to-do list — keeps piling up. So how do we actually do it all without completely running ourselves into the ground? Enter Julissa Prado. As the founder of Rizos Curls, the self-funded, multimillion-dollar haircare brand rooted in culture and community, Prado knows what it means to build something meaningful while balancing all the other pieces of her life. In our first episode of Sin Vergüenza, she gets real about how she manages it all and why doing more doesn’t necessarily mean doing everything at once.

Prado shares the strategies, patience, boundaries, and yes, self-love that have helped her grow Rizos Curls while making space for herself along the way. From a grading system that helps her prioritize the items on her to-do list to only putting on her plate what she’d serve her own figurative daughter, she offers advice for anyone trying to build a career, pursue a dream, care for the people they love, and still have something left for themselves at the end of the day.

Welcome to Sin Vergüenza, where young Latinas come to figure life out without shame, judgment, or the pressure to have it all together.
